headline: Baking a unique value into the class name mints 1,000 one-off classes: goober needs 1.27 s to hydrate the page and 149 ms at the largest size, while the lanes that keep the value out of the selector never notice.

microbench.why: Every element carries a unique `translateX`, and the naive pattern puts that value into the class name, so no merger can ever hit a cache. `bamboo` at 1.64M renders/s, `next-yak-css` at 1.59M and `vanilla` at 1.58M avoid the trap because the value reaches the element as a custom property or an inline style instead of as part of a selector. `next-yak` at 789,000 routes it through a CSS variable on a wrapper, which costs 0.743 ms of lib self-time. The pattern's real price lands on `goober` at 166,000 and `panda-props` at 157,000, which mint and insert a rule for every element.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css` at 1,349 req/s and `bamboo` at 1,177 lead. `goober` at 152 req/s and `panda-props` at 135 finish roughly an order below, because a thousand fresh rules get constructed inside every request.

attribution.why: `bamboo` at 0.742 ms, `next-yak-css` at 0.800 ms and `vanilla` at 0.801 ms hold the floor with no library at render. `next-yak` at 1.39 ms carries 0.743 ms of lib self-time for the variable wrapper. The pattern's cost gathers at the far end: 4.50 ms of lib time for `styled-components`, 6.04 ms for `goober`, and for the Panda lanes it lands in the component instead, 5.14 ms and 8.03 ms.

hydrate.why: `goober` needs 1,265 ms, more than ten times the next-slowest lane, because hydration re-inserts a thousand unique rules into the client sheet. Seven lanes finish between 45.1 ms and 49.8 ms. This single number is why the naive pattern earns a case of its own.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

inp.why: Ten lanes answer between 7.3 ms and 7.8 ms, since the interaction touches one element and mints no new classes. `panda-props` at 28.6 ms, `panda` at 22.2 ms and `goober` at 21.5 ms still pay, because their per-instance rule generation runs again on the re-render.

mount.why: `goober` at 1,241 ms is the outlier again, on the same mechanism as hydration. Eight lanes mount between 60.1 ms and 65.5 ms.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane at 0.078 ms to 0.181 ms. A thousand unique classes cost at insertion time rather than at match time, which is why this axis stays flat while hydrate and mount blow out.

payload.why: A thousand unique class names have to be written down somewhere. `vanilla` ships 5,502 gz B with the values in inline styles, while `emotion` reaches 39.4 kB and `styled-components` 35.5 kB, six to seven times the floor, because every distinct rule lands in both the sheet and the markup.

nsweep.why: `goober` at 149 ms against 2.53 ms for `next-yak-css` is a factor of 59, and it widens with the count, since each new element is a new rule. `next-yak` at 5.94 ms and `next-yak-nofold` at 5.06 ms are close together, because the CSS variable is the cost rather than the wrapper.

crossCase: The Examples `dyn-fair` and `dyn-inline` shown below take this workload two other ways. In `dyn-fair` every lane uses its own best practice, which for a library with no native dynamic-value support means a hand-written split of static class from inline style; that lifts `goober` from 166,000 to 945,000 renders/s and `panda` from 222,000 to 1.00M. next-yak ships that separation as a compiler feature, so nobody writes it; elsewhere the same result is developer discipline applied to every dynamic value, on every component, indefinitely. The naive pattern measured here is what a codebase gets when nobody pays that cost.
